query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the effective particle velocity by using a longer spray distance (approximately 300–350 mm) with the HVAF-i7 torch will overcome the thickness limitation while still producing a coating with low in-flight oxidation and good mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with 15–45 μm particle size, as demonstrated by optimal deposition on the HVAF-M3 system.
generation.intervention: Adjust the HVAF-i7 deposition process by increasing the spray stand-off distance to around 300–350 mm to boost particle velocity.
generation.conditions: Deposition using the HVAF-i7 torch with the modified spray distance in a configuration compatible with small internal diameters (as little as 120 mm); high-temperature thermal-barrier service conditions requiring both adhesion and oxidation resistance.
generation.structural_mediator: The higher particle velocity at an increased spray distance enhances splat formation and inter-splat bonding, resulting in denser and thicker bond-coat layers without compromising oxidation resistance.
generation.mechanism: A longer stand-off distance allows powder particles more time to accelerate, similar to conventional MCrAlY systems where higher velocities improved deposition efficiency. This increased kinetic energy promotes better substrate impact and coating buildup, thereby increasing thickness while maintaining quality.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant improvement in deposit thickness relative to the baseline HVAF-i7 process (which produces acceptable quality but insufficient thickness), while preserving minimal as-sprayed oxidation and adhesion suitable for high-temperature service.
generation.baseline: HVAF-i7 deposited coatings from 15–45 μm powder at the current (shorter) spray distance, which result in acceptable coating quality but inadequate thickness.
generation.boundary: This intervention should be effective provided that the increased flight time does not induce excessive oxidation and that other process parameters (e.g., powder composition, gas flow) remain controlled. It may be less effective if the ambient oxygen exposure during the extended flight leads to deteriorated coating properties.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the thickness gain is uncertain and may depend on the interplay of spray distance, particle temperature, and oxidation kinetics; experimental optimization is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of HVAF-i7 deposition experiments where the spray stand-off distance is systematically varied (e.g., 250, 300, 350, and 400 mm) while keeping the powder feedstock, torch power, and gas settings constant. Compare the coating thickness, microstructure, and oxidation levels.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing the spray distance to 300–350 mm does not produce a statistically significant increase in coating thickness compared to the baseline or if it results in unacceptable levels of oxidation or degraded adhesion, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 4 shows the difference in the properties based on the spraying distance. As the spraying distance increases, the average thickness of the coatings slightly decreases due to a stronger scattering of the particles on the longer path. An increase in the spraying distance results in an increase in coating porosity. Porosity depends on the temperature and kinetic energy of the particles []. Particles sprayed from a longer distance have a lower kinetic energy when they strike the substrate, which results in increased porosity. High temperatures and exposure to oxygen lead to the in-flight oxidation of particles; the smaller particles undergo more severe oxidation. With an increase in the spraying distance, the particles are exposed to oxygen for a longer time, which leads to an increased content of oxides (Figure 4d). As the particles oxidize with the formation of alumina, BCC solid solution loses aluminum, which is reflected in a decrease in its lattice parameter (Figure 3b). It is known [] that when Al concentration in FeCoNiCrAlMo0.5 is lower than 10%, FCC solid solution becomes preferable to BCC. The conventional principle of ESED is the generation of sparks when the anode and cathode come into contact, resulting in a very high local temperature that causes the anode electrode material to melt, transfer, and solidify onto the substrate. Similarly, when ESED is performed with powders, the powder particle in contact with the cathode substrate can be considered as the cathode during the powder deposition process. The high temperatures during the spark cause the powders to melt, fuse together, and solidify onto the substrate to form coating. In the ESPD process, when the electrode contacts with the dried powder slurry, the sparks are generated immediately. The slurry that has dark, rough, non-reflective surface starts burning, and transfer to a layer coating that has of silver, bright, and continuous surface.
